tagline: A farewell letter in Peter's name urging believers to grow in godliness, trust the apostolic witness, reject false teachers, and wait for the day of the Lord.
overview:
Second Peter presents itself as the last words of the apostle Peter, written in the knowledge that his death is near. It has three movements. First, Peter reminds his readers that God's power has given them everything they need for life and godliness, and he urges them to add virtue upon virtue to their faith, grounding his message in what he saw and heard on the mountain of the transfiguration and in the sure word of the prophets. Second, he warns at length against false teachers who will arise within the church, greedy and sensual, promising freedom while enslaved themselves, and he assures readers that God knows how to rescue the godly and judge the wicked, as he did in the flood and at Sodom. Third, he answers scoffers who mock the promise of Christ's coming because nothing seems to change: God is not slow but patient, the day of the Lord will come, and believers look for a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells.

The letter is short, urgent, and often neglected. It is also among the most debated books of the New Testament, both for its authorship and for its close relationship to the letter of Jude. Its lasting contributions are considerable: a vision of salvation as sharing in the divine nature, one of Scripture's clearest statements about how prophecy came from God, a warning that the church's worst dangers can come from inside it, and a patient answer to the question every generation asks, why the Lord has not yet returned.
author:
The letter claims to come from “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). It refers to Jesus' prediction of Peter's death (1:14; compare John 21:18-19), claims eyewitness presence at the transfiguration (1:16-18), calls itself Peter's second letter (3:1), and names Paul as “our beloved brother” (3:15). The traditional view accepts this at face value.

No New Testament book's authorship has been more questioned, and the doubts are ancient. Eusebius in the fourth century listed 2 Peter among the disputed books, reporting that it had not been received as canonical by all though many had found it useful, and Jerome noted that many rejected it because its style differed from 1 Peter. Modern scholars who judge it pseudonymous, now a large majority of critical scholarship, point to several features: its Greek is ornate and quite unlike 1 Peter; it seems to use Jude; it refers to a collection of Paul's letters and places them alongside the other Scriptures (3:15-16); it speaks of a time when the fathers have died (3:4); and it takes the form of a testament, a farewell speech genre often written in the name of a famous figure after his death. On this view, a follower of Peter wrote in his name to apply his authority to a new crisis, and first readers may have recognized the convention.

Those who defend Petrine authorship respond that Peter may have used a different secretary than Silvanus, or written this letter himself; that the testament form can be used by a real person facing death; that Paul's letters were being copied and gathered early; that the fathers of 3:4 may be the Old Testament patriarchs; and that the early church, which rejected other writings bearing Peter's name, did eventually receive this one. The letter was included in Athanasius's list of New Testament books in AD 367 and has been part of the canon of nearly all churches since.
date: If Peter wrote it, the letter comes shortly before his death in Rome under Nero, most likely around AD 64 to 68, and after 1 Peter. Those who regard it as pseudonymous generally date it between about AD 80 and 130, often in the early second century, making it perhaps the latest book of the New Testament. The relationship to Jude (whose own date is uncertain) and the reference to Paul's letters as a known body of writing are the main factors in the later dating. The earliest surviving manuscript containing it, a papyrus known as P72 from about the third or fourth century, includes 1 and 2 Peter and Jude.
setting:
The letter does not name its readers' location, but it assumes they received Peter's earlier letter (3:1), which would place them among the churches of Asia Minor addressed in 1 Peter, and that they knew some of Paul's letters (3:15-16). They are largely Gentile believers living in a Greek-speaking world. The letter uses vocabulary familiar to Greek moral philosophy, such as virtue, self-control, and godliness, and even speaks of sharing in the divine nature, borrowing the language of its culture to express the gospel.

The pressing danger is internal. Teachers within the churches are denying the Lord's return and future judgment, and are using freedom as a cover for sensual indulgence and greed. Their skepticism about Christ's coming may reflect Greek philosophical doubts about divine intervention in a stable universe (everything continues as it always has, 3:4), and their moral looseness may be a distorted version of Christian freedom. The letter's answer rests on history (God has intervened before, in the flood and at Sodom), on eyewitness testimony, and on the character of God.
purpose: Second Peter aims to secure the readers in the truth they already know. The author says repeatedly that he is reminding them (1:12-15; 3:1-2), so that after his departure they will remember. He wants them to grow in grace and knowledge, to recognize and reject false teachers, and to hold to the promise of Christ's return with holy and patient lives. The letter closes with a summary of its purpose: to be on guard, not carried away by error, and to “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).
story: Second Peter looks back to the transfiguration, when the Father's voice declared Jesus his beloved Son, and further back to the flood, the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the prophet Balaam. It looks forward to the end of the story, the day of the Lord, the dissolving of the present heavens and earth, and a new heaven and new earth where righteousness dwells, a hope drawn from Isaiah 65-66 and developed in Revelation 21-22. Within the New Testament it reflects the transition from the apostolic generation to the churches that must carry on after the apostles have died, relying on the apostles' writings and the prophetic Scriptures.
christ: Second Peter's opening calls Jesus “our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:1), one of the New Testament's plainest statements of his deity, and the letter repeatedly names him Lord and Savior. The transfiguration stands at its center: the apostles saw his majesty and heard the Father say, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (1:17). Christ's coming in power is the hope the false teachers deny and the letter defends, and the knowledge of Christ is the source of all growth in godliness. The false teachers are condemned precisely for “denying the Master who bought them” (2:1), a phrase that presents Christ as the Lord who purchased his people. The letter ends with a doxology addressed to Christ himself.
reading:
Read 2 Peter as a farewell testament: a leader facing death gathers what matters most and passes it on. Chapter 1 is its positive heart, chapter 2 its sustained warning, chapter 3 its defense of hope. Chapter 2 is full of vivid denunciation, which can feel harsh, but it serves the protection of vulnerable believers from teachers who exploit them.

Reading 2 Peter alongside Jude is illuminating. Jude 4-18 and 2 Peter 2:1-3:3 share much of their content, order, and imagery: false teachers who deny the Master, the angels who sinned, Sodom and Gomorrah, Balaam, waterless springs and clouds, and scoffers in the last days. Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude, because Jude's version is more compact and vivid, and because 2 Peter omits Jude's references to Jewish writings outside the Old Testament (1 Enoch and the dispute over Moses' body). Others argue Jude used 2 Peter, noting that 2 Peter predicts the false teachers in the future tense while Jude says the apostles foretold them; still others propose a common source. Borrowing between inspired writers would not have troubled ancient readers. Watch also for the letter's careful account of prophecy (1:19-21) and its famous saying that with the Lord a day is like a thousand years (3:8), which is about God's patience, not a formula for calculating dates.

structure.title: Growing in godliness
structure.summary: After the greeting, Peter reminds readers that God has given them everything for life and godliness, calls them to add virtue to faith, and explains that he writes as a reminder before his death.

structure.title: Eyewitness and prophetic testimony
structure.summary: The apostles did not follow clever myths: they saw Christ's majesty on the holy mountain, and the prophetic word came from God as men were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

structure.title: False teachers and their judgment
structure.summary: False teachers will arise, as false prophets did in Israel. God judged fallen angels, the ancient world, and Sodom while rescuing Noah and Lot, and he will judge these greedy and sensual teachers.

structure.title: The day of the Lord
structure.summary: Scoffers deny Christ's coming, but God's word created and judged the world, God is patient, and the day will come. Believers wait in holiness for a new heaven and earth and grow in grace and knowledge.

themes.title: Knowledge of God and Christ
themes.body: Knowledge runs through the letter, from the greeting (1:2) to the final charge (3:18). It is not esoteric information of the kind false teachers claimed, but personal, growing acquaintance with Christ that produces a godly life. Knowledge that yields no fruit, the letter warns, leaves a person nearsighted and forgetful.

themes.title: Growth in virtue
themes.body: The chain of virtues in 1:5-7, from faith to love, shows the Christian life as active growth grounded in God's gift. God's power has already given what is needed; believers respond by making every effort. The aim is a life that confirms one's calling and election and ends in a rich welcome into Christ's eternal kingdom.

themes.title: The reliability of the apostolic and prophetic word
themes.body: Against teachers who dismissed Christ's return as myth, 2 Peter appeals to two witnesses: the apostles who saw Christ's glory, and the prophets whose words came from God by the Spirit. The letter also places Paul's letters beside the other Scriptures, an early sign of the church recognizing its apostolic writings.

themes.title: Judgment and rescue
themes.body: Chapter 2 traces a double pattern through Genesis: God judges the ungodly and rescues the righteous, as he judged the ancient world and saved Noah, and destroyed Sodom and delivered Lot. The pattern assures believers that God's judgment on false teachers is certain and that he knows how to rescue his own.

themes.title: Patience and the coming day
themes.body: The apparent delay of Christ's return is God's patience, giving time for repentance. The day of the Lord will come like a thief, and the present order will give way to a new heaven and a new earth. The right response is holy and godly living, eager expectation, and peace.

keyChapters.why: God's provision for life and godliness, the ladder of virtues, the transfiguration testimony, and the classic statement on how prophecy came from God.
The longest New Testament warning against false teachers, closely parallel to Jude.
The answer to scoffers about Christ's delayed return, the promise of a new heaven and earth, and the reference to Paul's letters as Scripture.

parts.body:
2 Peter is a short letter, three chapters, and it reads in about ten minutes. It presents itself as Peter's farewell, written when he knew his death was near: “I know that this tent will soon be laid aside” (1:14). Like a man saying his last words to people he loves, he gathers what matters most and passes it on, so that ‘after my departure’ they will remember (1:15).

It moves in three steps. First, a reminder of what God has given. His power has given believers “everything we need for life and godliness” (1:3), and they are to grow, adding goodness, knowledge, self-control and love to their faith. Peter grounds this in what he saw: Jesus' glory on ‘the holy mountain’ (1:18), and the word of the prophets.

Second, a long warning. False teachers will arise inside the church, greedy and self-indulgent, promising freedom while they themselves are slaves (2:19). God judged in the past and rescued in the past, in the flood and at Sodom, and he still ‘knows how to rescue the godly’ (2:9).

Third, an answer to people who mocked: ‘Where is the promise of His coming?’ (3:4). God is not slow. He is patient, “not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (3:9). The day of the Lord will come, and believers look for “a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells” (3:13).

2 Peter is often neglected. It is also one of the most debated books of the New Testament, above all over who wrote it. These notes say honestly why many doubt that Peter wrote it, and why others hold that he did. They do not choose, beyond receiving the letter, as the church has, as Scripture.

The letter claims to come from “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). It speaks of Jesus' words about Peter's death (1:14; compare John 21:18-19). It says the writer was on the mountain when Jesus was transfigured (1:16-18). It calls itself his second letter (3:1), and it calls Paul “our beloved brother” (3:15). The traditional view takes these words at face value: Peter wrote it near the end of his life.

No book of the New Testament has had its authorship questioned more, and the doubts are old. In the 300s the historian Eusebius listed 2 Peter among the disputed books: not all had received it, though many found it useful. Jerome noted that many rejected it because its style was not like 1 Peter. Even John Calvin, in the 1500s, doubted that Peter wrote it, though he accepted it as Scripture.

Today a large majority of critical scholars think it was written after Peter's death, in his name, by someone who wanted to apply his teaching to a new crisis. Their reasons: its Greek is ornate and very different from 1 Peter's; it seems to use the letter of Jude; it speaks of a collection of Paul's letters and sets them beside ‘the rest of the Scriptures’ (3:15-16), which suggests a later time; it speaks of a time when ‘our fathers fell asleep’ (3:4), as if the first generation had died; and it takes the form of a testament, a farewell speech, a kind of writing often composed in a famous person's name after his death. On this view the first readers may have recognised the form for what it was.

Those who hold that Peter wrote it reply that he may have used a different helper from Silvanus, or written this one himself; that a real person facing death can write a farewell; that Paul's letters were copied and gathered early; that ‘the fathers’ of 3:4 may be Israel's patriarchs; and that the early church, which rejected other writings that carried Peter's name, in the end received this one.

These notes do not choose. They call the writer ‘Peter’, as the letter does. The church came to receive it as Scripture: Athanasius counted it in the New Testament in 367, and nearly all churches have read it as Scripture since. Doubting who held the pen and receiving the book as God's word are not the same question, and Christians have held the second firmly while differing on the first.

If Peter wrote it, the letter comes shortly before his death in Rome under Nero, most likely between AD 64 and 68, and after 1 Peter. Those who think it was written later in his name usually date it between about AD 80 and 130, often early in the second century, which would make it perhaps the last book of the New Testament to be written. The oldest surviving copy is a papyrus known as P72, from about the 200s or 300s, which also holds 1 Peter and Jude.

The letter does not say where its readers lived. If it is the ‘second letter’ to the same people as 1 Peter (3:1), they were in the churches of Asia Minor. They knew some of Paul's letters (3:15-16). Most of them were Gentiles in a Greek-speaking world, and the letter speaks their language, using words that Greek moral teachers used, like ‘virtue’, ‘self-control’ and ‘godliness’.

The danger is inside. Teachers in the churches were saying that Christ would not come back and that there would be no judgment. Some Greek thinkers held that the gods did not step into human affairs or judge wrongdoing, and that the world went on as it always had. Whether or not the teachers drew on such ideas, their message sounded the same: ‘everything continues as it has from the beginning’ (3:4), so live as you like.

What God has given, and growing in it (chapter 1). A greeting to those with ‘a faith as precious as ours’. God's power and promises, and a chain of virtues from faith to love. Peter's coming death and his wish to leave a reminder. Two witnesses: the apostles who saw Jesus' glory on the mountain, and the prophets, whose words came from God.

False teachers (chapter 2). They will come, as false prophets came in Israel. God judged the angels who sinned, the world of Noah's day, and Sodom and Gomorrah, and he rescued Noah and Lot. The teachers are greedy and proud, like Balaam. They promise freedom and are slaves.

The day of the Lord (chapter 3). Scoffers ask where the promise is. Peter answers: God's word judged the world before; a day with the Lord is like a thousand years; his delay is patience; the day will come like a thief. So live holy lives, look for the new heaven and new earth, read Paul with care, and grow in grace.

parts.h: Sharing the divine nature, and growing
parts.body:
Peter makes one of the boldest promises in the New Testament: through God's promises believers “may become partakers of the divine nature” (1:4). Christians have understood it in more than one way. Orthodox teaching draws on it for theosis, union with God by grace, in which believers share God's life without ever ceasing to be creatures. Western churches usually read it as sharing God's holy character and his life that does not die, through union with Christ. All agree it does not mean becoming God in essence.

Then Peter asks for effort. “For this very reason, make every effort to add to your faith virtue” (1:5), and he builds a ladder that climbs from faith to love. God's gift comes first; effort answers it. Without growth, a believer becomes ‘nearsighted to the point of blindness’, forgetting he has been cleansed (1:9).

“Therefore, brothers, strive to make your calling and election sure” (1:10). Christians read this in line with their wider views of God's choosing, set out in the notes on 1 Peter 1:1-2 and 2 Peter 2:20-22. Reformed Christians read it as confirming in life what God has already done. Arminian and Wesleyan Christians read it as a call to persevere in a calling that can be abandoned. Both agree that Peter is not asking anyone to earn God's choice, and that he writes to give assurance, not fear: ‘you will never stumble’ (1:10). These notes do not choose.

parts.h: The prophets, the apostles, and Scripture
parts.body:
Some were calling the apostles' message about Christ's coming a myth. Peter answers: “For we did not follow cleverly devised fables”, he writes; “we were eyewitnesses of His majesty” (1:16). He heard the Father's voice on the mountain: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (1:17).

Then he points to the prophets. Their word is “a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (1:19). And he says how it came: “For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:21). The word ‘carried along’ is used in Acts of a ship driven by the wind. The prophets were moved by the Spirit while still speaking as themselves.

The verse before is read in two ways: “no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation” (1:20). Many take it to be about where prophecy came from: not the prophet's own ideas. Others take it to be about how it is read: not by private whim, but with the Spirit and the church. Catholic and Orthodox teaching has often drawn on the second reading for the church's teaching office; Protestant teaching stresses that Scripture is its own best interpreter. All agree that Scripture must not be twisted to suit ourselves.

And near the end, Peter speaks of Paul's letters, which “ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures” (3:16). It is one of the earliest signs that the church read the apostles' letters as Scripture.

The letter's first line calls Jesus “our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:1). In the Greek, the grammar most naturally applies both titles, ‘God’ and ‘Savior’, to Jesus. It is one of the plainest statements in the New Testament that Jesus is God. The letter's last line says the same in another way. It gives glory to Jesus Christ ‘both now and to the day of eternity’ (3:18), praise the Bible elsewhere gives to God alone.

At the centre stands the transfiguration. Peter, James and John saw Jesus' glory on a mountain and heard the Father say, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (1:17). The Gospels tell it too (Mark 9:2-8). For Peter it was a preview and a pledge of Christ's coming in power. The Gospels do not name the mountain; later tradition named Mount Tabor, and some modern scholars suggest Mount Hermon. Peter calls it simply ‘the holy mountain’ because of what happened there.

Jesus is also ‘the Master who bought them’ (2:1), the owner who paid for his people. To deny him is to rebel against the one to whom they belong. And knowing him is the source of all growth: “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).

parts.h: False teachers, and the letter of Jude
parts.body:
Chapter 2 is the letter's sharpest. It warns that the worst danger to the church can come from inside it: teachers who ‘secretly introduce destructive heresies’, who will ‘exploit you with deceptive words’ for money (2:1, 3), who ‘seduce the unstable’ (2:14), and who promise freedom while being ‘slaves to depravity’ (2:19). Its fierce words protect the people such teachers prey on.

Peter gives three examples of God's judgment, and two of rescue. God did not spare ‘the angels when they sinned’ (2:4). The word for casting them ‘deep into hell’ is tartaroō, from Tartarus, a name Greek stories gave to the deepest prison of the underworld, and which Jewish writers of the time used for where rebel angels were held. Most readers think Peter means the beings of Genesis 6:1-4, as Jewish tradition read that passage; the word describes holding before judgment, not the final state. God judged the world in the flood but kept Noah; he destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah but rescued Lot. So ‘the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials’ (2:9).

Much of 2:1 to 3:3 is very close to the short letter of Jude: the same images, in much the same order. Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude, because Jude's version is shorter and sharper, and because 2 Peter leaves out Jude's direct use of 1 Enoch and of the dispute over Moses' body, writings outside the Old Testament. Others think Jude used 2 Peter, or that both drew on a common source. These notes do not choose. Borrowing between writers would not have troubled ancient readers.

These warnings are about teachers who exploit people. If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith; the Corinthians were taken in too. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

‘Where is the promise of His coming?’ the scoffers ask. ‘Everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation’ (3:4). Peter answers in four ways. The world has not always gone on unchanged: God's word made it, and by water the world of that time ‘perished in the flood’ (3:5-6). God does not count time as we do: “With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day” (3:8). The delay is patience. And the day will come suddenly, ‘like a thief’ (3:10).

“With the Lord a day is like a thousand years” is about God's patience. It is not a formula for working out dates. Peter gives no date, and he offers no timetable or scheme of the last days.

“The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (3:9). Many read this as God's sincere desire for every person to turn and live. Others, especially in the Reformed tradition, read such words in a narrower sense, as they read ‘who wants everyone to be saved’ in 1 Timothy 2:4, and the notes there set out how. Traditions explain these words differently, but all of them read them as sincere, and all agree that the time before Christ comes is a time of mercy.

Verse 10 is hard. “The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.” Here the manuscripts differ. Older translations followed later manuscripts that say the earth and its works ‘will be burned up’. Most modern translations follow early manuscripts with a word that means ‘will be found’, which the BSB renders ‘laid bare’: the fire of judgment exposes everything to God's sight. Christians read the passage in two main ways. Some hold that the present universe will be wholly destroyed and replaced by a new creation. Others hold that it will be purged and renewed, as the flood judged the world without abolishing the earth, and they point to Romans 8, where creation itself will be set free. These notes do not choose. Both agree on Peter's point: the present order is not permanent, everything will be judged, and God has promised a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells.

Peter speaks of the flood (3:5-6; 2:5) to show that God has acted in the world before. These notes take no position on the age of the earth or on how widely the flood's waters spread. Christians who share the same faith differ on those questions, and Peter's point does not depend on them.

Peter reads the Old Testament as a record of God acting in history. He names Noah, ‘a preacher of righteousness’ (2:5), and the eight saved in the ark. He names Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot, ‘a righteous man’ who was distressed by what he saw (2:7-8). He names Balaam, the prophet who loved money and was rebuked by his donkey (2:15-16; Numbers 22). He quotes Proverbs: “A dog returns to its vomit” (2:22; Proverbs 26:11). And his line about a thousand years echoes a psalm: “For in Your sight a thousand years are but a day that passes” (Psalm 90:4).

The hope of ‘a new heaven and a new earth’ (3:13) is Isaiah's: “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). And ‘the Day of the Lord’ is the prophets' name for the day God comes to judge and to put things right.

It is not a timetable for the end. A thousand years like a day is about God's patience, not arithmetic, and the letter gives no date.

It is not a position on the age of the earth or the extent of the flood. Peter uses the flood to show that God acts in history.

It is not a licence to call every teacher you disagree with a false teacher. Its marks are greed, exploiting people, sensual indulgence, seducing the unstable, and denying Christ and the judgment.

It is not a reason for despair about the world. Its last picture is a new heaven and a new earth ‘where righteousness dwells’.

And it is not a weaker book because its author is debated. The church received it as Scripture, and its call is plain: “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).

Read it as a farewell: someone who knows he has little time, telling people he loves what they must not forget. It takes about ten minutes.

Chapter 1 is its heart, chapter 2 its warning, chapter 3 its hope. Read chapter 2 beside the letter of Jude, and notice what each includes. Read chapter 3 with Isaiah 65 and Romans 8 open.

Notice the words that return: ‘knowledge’, ‘remind’, ‘promise’, ‘godliness’, ‘patience’.

Where readers differ, on who wrote it, on the divine nature, on election, on the burning or laying bare of the earth, read more than one view before you settle, and hold your own view as one who may yet be taught.

And let it ask its questions. Are you growing, or standing still? Whom are you listening to, and what do they want from you? And do you think of God's patience as slowness, or as mercy?

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

words.line: Greek epignōsis, full or personal knowledge: knowing God and Jesus, which bears fruit in life (1:2-3, 8; 3:18).
Greek eusebeia, a word Greek moral teachers used for reverence; for Peter, a life shaped by God (1:3, 6-7).
Greek theias phuseōs: sharing God's life by grace, never becoming God in essence (1:4).
Greek aretē, excellence or goodness, a favourite word of Greek moral teaching (1:3, 5).
Greek epoptēs, one who has seen with his own eyes (1:16).
Greek pherō, used in Acts of a ship driven by the wind: the prophets moved by the Spirit (1:21).
Greek despotēs, the owner of a slave. Christ is the Master who bought his people (2:1).
The Greek name for the deepest prison of the underworld, used for where the angels who sinned are held (2:4).
Greek eleutheria. The false teachers promise it while slaves to whatever masters them (2:19).
Greek parousia, a ruler's arrival; used for Christ's return (3:4, 12).
Greek makrothumeō, to be long-tempered: holding back from anger to give time to turn (3:9, 15).
Greek stoicheia: the building blocks of the world, or the sun, moon and stars (3:10, 12).

Sodom and Gomorrah are destroyed and Lot is rescued (Genesis 19; 2 Peter 2:6-7).

Peter, James and John see Jesus transfigured on a mountain (Mark 9:2-8; 2 Peter 1:16-18).
The great fire of Rome; Nero blames the Christians.
The letter is written shortly before Peter's death in Rome, if Peter wrote it.
The date most often given by scholars who think it was written later in Peter's name.

Athanasius counts 2 Peter in the New Testament.

places.name: Sodom and Gomorrah
places.line: The cities God condemned in Lot's day, ‘reducing them to ashes’ (2:6; Genesis 19). Where they stood is not known. Drawn at the south end of the Dead Sea, one of the places proposed, roughly.

teaching.mapNote: 2 Peter names only one place on earth: Sodom and Gomorrah (2:6). Where they stood is not known; they are drawn roughly at the south end of the Dead Sea, one of the places proposed. The letter does not say where it was written or where its readers lived, and it does not name ‘the holy mountain’ (1:18).
